topics.name: Rhode Island
topics.kicker: Smallest state · Roger Williams’s colony of religious freedom
topics.briefing: Rhode Island is the smallest state, but its history is full of rebels. Roger Williams founded Providence in 1636 after Massachusetts banished him, and the colony became a haven for people of many faiths. Its colonists burned a British ship in the Gaspee Affair, and Samuel Slater built America’s first successful water-powered cotton-spinning mill there, but it was the last of the 13 original states to approve the Constitution.
topics.answerHtml: Rhode Island (accept Rhode Island and Providence Plantations; do not accept “Providence”)
accept: colony of rhode island and providence plantations
state of rhode island and providence plantations

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: A 1663 royal charter from King Charles II called this colony a “lively experiment” in full religious freedom, and that charter served as its constitution until 1843. John Clarke spent years in London winning that charter for this colony.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this colony founded by Roger Williams, which became the smallest U.S. state.

tossups.p: This state and Connecticut were the only two states that never ratified the 18th Amendment, which created national Prohibition. The painter Gilbert Stuart, whose portrait of George Washington appears on the one-dollar bill, was born here in 1755.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this smallest U.S. state, home to the cities of Providence and Newport.

tossups.p: George Washington promised “to bigotry no sanction, to persecution no assistance” in a 1790 letter to the Jewish congregation in this state’s city of Newport. That congregation’s Touro Synagogue is the oldest surviving synagogue building in the United States.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this smallest U.S. state, founded as a colony by Roger Williams.

tossups.p: In 1772, merchant John Brown led a group of colonists who rowed out and burned the British customs schooner _Gaspee_ after it ran aground while chasing another ship in this colony’s waters. A royal commission later failed to find anyone willing to name the attackers.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this New England colony, later the smallest state, whose capital is Providence.

tossups.p: Samuel Slater memorized the designs of British textile machines and then, with money from the Quaker merchant Moses Brown, built a water-powered cotton-spinning mill in this state’s village of Pawtucket [“puh-TUCK-it”]. People in Britain called him “Slater the Traitor.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this New England state where Slater helped start the American Industrial Revolution.

tossups.p: In the 1840s, Thomas Dorr led a rebellion because this state kept using its 1663 royal charter as its constitution, and only men who owned land could vote. Supporters of his “People’s Constitution” even elected Dorr governor, so this state briefly had two rival governments.
tossups.r: The rebellion led to a new state constitution in 1843. For 10 points, name this New England state whose capital is Providence.

tossups.p: Anne Hutchinson’s followers founded Portsmouth on Aquidneck [“uh-KWID-nek”] Island, the island this colony was named for, after Massachusetts banished her. William Coddington and John Clarke later founded Newport at the other end of that island.
tossups.r: Roger Williams had already founded Providence nearby. For 10 points, name this colony, which became the smallest state.

tossups.p: On May 4, 1776, two months before the Declaration of Independence, this colony’s legislature renounced its loyalty to King George III. Years later, it refused to send delegates to the Constitutional Convention and became the last of the thirteen original states to ratify the Constitution.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this state, which finally ratified in 1790 and is the smallest of the fifty states.

tossups.p: Oliver Hazard Perry, the hero of the Battle of Lake Erie, and his younger brother Matthew, who opened Japan to American trade, were both born in this state. Earlier, Nathanael Greene of this state became one of George Washington’s most trusted generals.
tossups.r: Greene and Roger Williams represent it in the National Statuary Hall Collection. For 10 points, name this New England state whose capital is Providence.

tossups.p: In 1778, this state’s 1st Regiment, which included many Black and Native American soldiers, held its ground against repeated attacks during a battle on Aquidneck Island. A French fleet had come to help the Americans in that campaign but sailed away before the battle.
tossups.r: That battle followed a failed attempt to retake Newport from the British. For 10 points, name this New England state, whose capital is Providence.

tossups.p: Gilded Age millionaires built enormous summer “cottages” in this state’s city of Newport, including The Breakers, built for Cornelius Vanderbilt II. Newport is also home to the Naval War College and the International Tennis Hall of Fame.
tossups.r: Its capital is Providence. For 10 points, name this smallest of the fifty states.

tossups.p: The Ivy League college in this state was renamed in 1804 for Nicholas Brown Jr., a merchant whose family had long supported it. That college, first founded in 1764, had moved to this state’s capital in 1770.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this state, home to Brown University and the capital city of Providence.

tossups.p: This state’s town of Bristol claims the oldest continuous Fourth of July celebration in the country, first held in 1785. Coffee milk was named its official state drink in 1993, and its flag shows a golden anchor above the one-word motto “Hope.”
tossups.r: Its capital is Providence. For 10 points, name this smallest U.S. state, nicknamed the Ocean State.

tossups.p: Jewish families settled in this colony’s town of Newport in the 1650s, and Quakers were allowed to worship freely there while other New England colonies punished them. Its founder had been banished from Massachusetts in 1635 for spreading “new and dangerous opinions.”
tossups.r: Critics called it “Rogues’ Island.” For 10 points, name this colony founded by Roger Williams.

tossups.p: Stephen Hopkins and William Ellery signed the Declaration of Independence for this colony, and Hopkins’s brother Esek became the first commander in chief of the Continental Navy. Stephen Hopkins had earlier served several terms as this colony’s governor.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this colony founded by Roger Williams, later the smallest state.

clues.t: Smallest U.S. state by area; nicknamed the Ocean State
Founded by Roger Williams, who started Providence in 1636 after Massachusetts banished him
Capital: Providence, at the head of Narragansett Bay; another famous city is Newport
A colony of religious freedom that welcomed Baptists, Quakers, and Jews
Last of the 13 original states to ratify the Constitution (1790); it sent no delegates to the Constitutional Convention
Anne Hutchinson’s followers founded Portsmouth (1638) after Massachusetts banished her
Gaspee Affair (1772): colonists led by John Brown burned the British customs schooner _Gaspee_ after it ran aground
Samuel Slater built a water-powered cotton-spinning mill at Pawtucket from British designs he had memorized
Touro Synagogue in Newport (dedicated 1763) is the oldest surviving synagogue building in the United States
On May 4, 1776, its legislature renounced loyalty to King George III, two months before the Declaration of Independence
Home of Brown University (chartered 1764), an Ivy League school renamed for Nicholas Brown Jr. in 1804
Critics in Massachusetts called it “Rogues’ Island” because it took in religious outcasts
Roger Williams helped start the first Baptist church in America in Providence (1638)
Its flag shows a golden anchor and the one-word motto “Hope”
John Clarke won a 1663 royal charter from Charles II that called the colony a “lively experiment” in religious freedom; it served as the state constitution until 1843
Dorr Rebellion (1841–1842): Thomas Dorr’s “People’s Constitution” challenged the rule that only landowners could vote; two rival governments claimed power
George Washington’s 1790 letter to Newport’s Jewish congregation promised “to bigotry no sanction, to persecution no assistance”
Newport and Portsmouth sit on Aquidneck Island, which the colony was named for; William Coddington and John Clarke founded Newport (1639)
Quaker merchant Moses Brown paid for Slater’s mill; in Britain, Slater was called “Slater the Traitor”
With Connecticut, one of only two states that never ratified the 18th Amendment (Prohibition)
Painter Gilbert Stuart, whose portrait of Washington is on the one-dollar bill, was born there (1755)
Birthplace of naval officers Oliver Hazard Perry and Matthew Perry and of General Nathanael Greene
Its 1st Regiment, often called the “Black Regiment,” included many Black and Native American soldiers and fought in a 1778 battle on Aquidneck Island
Stephen Hopkins and William Ellery signed the Declaration for it; Esek Hopkins was the first commander in chief of the Continental Navy
Gilded Age “cottages” such as the Vanderbilts’ The Breakers stand in Newport, home of the Naval War College
Its name may come from Giovanni da Verrazzano comparing an island there to the Greek island of Rhodes
In 2020, voters approved dropping “and Providence Plantations” from its official state name

trap.title: Colony, city, or founder?
trap.body: Many Rhode Island tossups lean on Roger Williams and Providence, which have their own answer lines: Roger Williams is the man, and Providence is the capital city he founded in 1636. Neighbors cause trouble too: Massachusetts banished both Williams and Anne Hutchinson, and Thomas Hooker led his congregation from Massachusetts to found Hartford, Connecticut.
trap.fix: Listen for the noun. “This colony” or “this state” with the Gaspee, Slater’s mill, Touro Synagogue, the Dorr Rebellion, or the last ratification of the Constitution means Rhode Island; “this man” means Roger Williams; “this city” means Providence or Newport. The old official name, “Rhode Island and Providence Plantations,” is also fine, but “Providence” alone names a city.
trap.line: Real answer line: Rhode Island (accept Rhode Island and Providence Plantations)

topics.name: Roe v. Wade
topics.kicker: 1973 Supreme Court abortion ruling · Overruled by Dobbs in 2022
topics.briefing: _Roe v. Wade_ is one of the most famous and most debated Supreme Court cases in U.S. history. In 1973, the Court ruled 7–2 for “Jane Roe,” a Texas woman whose real name was Norma McCorvey, holding that a constitutional right to privacy covers a woman’s decision whether to have an abortion. In 2022, the Court overruled Roe in _Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization_, returning the question of abortion laws to the states.
topics.answerHtml: Roe v. Wade (prompt on “Roe” or “Wade” alone; do not accept “abortion”)
reject: dobbs v jackson womens health organization

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Sarah Weddington, who was only 26 when she first argued this case before the Supreme Court, and Linda Coffee represented its plaintiff, a Texas woman named Norma McCorvey. To protect her privacy, the plaintiff was given a pseudonym in this case.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1973 Supreme Court decision that was overruled by _Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization_.

tossups.p: The defendant in this case was a Texas district attorney whose office had prosecuted Jack Ruby, the man who shot Lee Harvey Oswald. That district attorney served Dallas County for more than thirty years.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1973 Supreme Court case about abortion and the right to privacy.

tossups.p: This case was argued twice before the Supreme Court, in December 1971 and October 1972, because Lewis Powell and William Rehnquist [“REN-kwist”] joined the Court after the first argument. In the 7–2 decision, Rehnquist and Byron White dissented.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1973 case about the right to privacy and abortion.

tossups.p: On the same day it decided this case, the Supreme Court also struck down parts of a Georgia law in a companion case, _Doe v. Bolton_, which was brought by a woman using the name “Mary Doe.” Justice Harry Blackmun wrote the majority opinions in both cases.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1973 decision that struck down a Texas law restricting abortion.

tossups.p: The author of this decision’s majority opinion had worked as a lawyer for the Mayo Clinic before Richard Nixon appointed him to the Supreme Court. That justice, Harry Blackmun, based this decision on a right to privacy.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1973 case that the Supreme Court overruled in 2022.

tossups.p: A 1992 joint opinion by Sandra Day O’Connor, Anthony Kennedy, and David Souter kept the core of this decision but replaced its trimester framework with an “undue burden” test. That case, _Planned Parenthood v. Casey_, involved a Pennsylvania law.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1973 decision about abortion, written by Harry Blackmun.

tossups.p: In May 2022, the news site _Politico_ published a leaked draft of a Supreme Court opinion that would overrule this decision. The final opinion, written by Samuel Alito, upheld a Mississippi law and returned the question of abortion laws to the states.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1973 case that was overruled in _Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization_.

tossups.p: This decision built on _Griswold v. Connecticut_, a 1965 case in which Justice William O. Douglas wrote that guarantees in the Bill of Rights have “penumbras” that create zones of privacy. Douglas also joined the majority in this decision.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1973 Supreme Court case that struck down a Texas abortion law.

tossups.p: The plaintiff in this case later revealed her identity, and in 1995 she announced that she had changed her views and would work with groups that opposed this decision. That plaintiff, Norma McCorvey, had used a pseudonym when the case began in Texas.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1973 Supreme Court case decided by a 7–2 vote.

tossups.p: This decision created a framework that divided pregnancy into three trimesters and allowed states to regulate abortion more as a pregnancy went on. Nineteen years later, the Supreme Court dropped that framework but kept the core of this decision.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1973 case named for a Texas plaintiff and a Dallas district attorney.

tossups.p: Chief Justice Warren Burger and Thurgood Marshall were among the seven justices in the majority in this decision, which was announced on January 22, 1973. Its majority opinion traced the history of laws on its subject back to ancient times, including ancient Greece and Rome.
tossups.r: It said a right to privacy covers a woman’s decision whether to have an abortion. For 10 points, name this case that the Supreme Court overruled in 2022.

tossups.p: The case that overruled this decision was named for Thomas Dobbs, Mississippi’s top state health officer, and a clinic in the state’s capital. That 2022 ruling said that the Constitution does not grant a right to abortion and left the question to the states.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1973 decision, written by Harry Blackmun, that the _Dobbs_ case overruled.

tossups.p: In 1970, a three-judge federal court in Dallas declared the law challenged in this case unconstitutional but did not order Texas to stop enforcing it. The Supreme Court then struck down that law, which banned abortion except to save the woman’s life.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1973 Supreme Court decision, written by Harry Blackmun, about the right to privacy.

tossups.p: The lower court in this case found a right to privacy in the Ninth Amendment, but the Supreme Court’s majority said that right was founded in the Fourteenth Amendment’s concept of personal liberty. Harry Blackmun wrote that majority opinion.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1973 case about abortion that the Court overruled in 2022.

tossups.p: When the Supreme Court overruled this decision in 2022, Stephen Breyer, Sonia Sotomayor, and Elena Kagan wrote a joint dissent, while Chief Justice John Roberts voted to uphold the state law but would not have overruled this decision entirely.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1973 decision that had recognized a constitutional right to abortion.

clues.t: 1973 Supreme Court case that recognized a constitutional right to abortion, based on a right to privacy
Overruled in 2022 by _Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization_, which returned the issue to the states
Struck down a Texas law that banned abortion except to save the woman’s life
Decided 7–2; Justice Harry Blackmun wrote the majority opinion
The plaintiff, “Jane Roe,” was a pseudonym for Norma McCorvey, a Texas woman
The defendant, Henry Wade, was the district attorney of Dallas County, Texas
Based the right to privacy on the Fourteenth Amendment’s Due Process Clause and its protection of “liberty”
Set up a trimester framework: the later in a pregnancy, the more a state could regulate abortion
_Planned Parenthood v. Casey_ (1992) kept the core of the ruling but replaced the trimester framework with an “undue burden” test
Built on _Griswold v. Connecticut_ (1965), which recognized a constitutional right to privacy
Justices Byron White and William Rehnquist dissented
Justice Samuel Alito wrote the 2022 majority opinion that overruled it
Lawyers Sarah Weddington and Linda Coffee brought the case; Weddington was 26 when she first argued it
Argued twice (1971 and 1972) because Lewis Powell and William Rehnquist joined the Court in between
Its companion case, _Doe v. Bolton_, decided the same day, struck down parts of a Georgia law
Henry Wade’s office had prosecuted Jack Ruby, the man who shot Lee Harvey Oswald
Blackmun, appointed by Richard Nixon, had been a lawyer for the Mayo Clinic
Chief Justice Warren Burger joined the majority; the decision was announced on January 22, 1973
Blackmun’s opinion traced the history of abortion laws back to ancient times, including ancient Greece and Rome
The lower court had found the right to privacy in the Ninth Amendment; the Supreme Court pointed to the Fourteenth instead
In _Griswold_, Justice William O. Douglas wrote that the Bill of Rights has “penumbras” that create zones of privacy
In 1995, Norma McCorvey announced she had changed her views and began working with groups opposed to the decision
_Casey_’s joint opinion was written by Sandra Day O’Connor, Anthony Kennedy, and David Souter; the case involved a Pennsylvania law
_Dobbs_ upheld a Mississippi law; it was named for Thomas Dobbs, the state health officer, and a clinic in Jackson

trap.title: Which abortion case?
trap.body: Three Supreme Court cases come up together. _Roe v. Wade_ (1973) recognized a constitutional right to abortion; _Planned Parenthood v. Casey_ (1992) kept that right but replaced Roe’s trimester framework with an “undue burden” test; and _Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization_ (2022) overruled both and returned the issue to the states. Answering only “abortion,” or naming the wrong case, will not get credit.
trap.fix: Listen for the year and the names: 1973, Harry Blackmun, “Jane Roe,” Henry Wade, Texas, and trimesters mean _Roe v. Wade_; 1992, Pennsylvania, and “undue burden” mean _Casey_; 2022, Mississippi, Samuel Alito, and the leaked draft mean _Dobbs_.
trap.line: Real answer line: Roe v. Wade (do not accept “abortion” alone)

topics.name: Ronald Reagan
topics.kicker: 40th U.S. President · Actor turned governor and Cold War leader
topics.briefing: Ronald Reagan was a radio sports announcer, a Hollywood actor, and president of the Screen Actors Guild before he became governor of California. As the 40th president, from 1981 to 1989, he cut income taxes, survived being shot just 69 days into his first term, and urged Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev to “tear down this wall” in Berlin. In 1987, the two leaders signed a treaty that eliminated a whole class of nuclear missiles.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: This actor’s line “Where’s the rest of me?”, from the film _Kings Row_, became the title of his first autobiography. He also played the football player George Gipp in _Knute Rockne, All American_, which gave him a lasting nickname.
tossups.r: He later served as governor of California. For 10 points, name this actor who became the 40th president.

tossups.p: As a young radio announcer in Des Moines, Iowa, this man described Chicago Cubs games that he re-created from short telegraph reports. Earlier, he had worked as a lifeguard in Dixon, Illinois, and graduated from Eureka College.
tossups.r: He later became a Hollywood actor. For 10 points, name this man who was elected president in 1980.

tossups.p: This man’s televised 1964 speech “A Time for Choosing,” given in support of Barry Goldwater’s presidential campaign, launched his own political career. He had switched from the Democratic Party to the Republican Party two years earlier.
tossups.r: Two years after that speech, he was elected governor of California. For 10 points, name this man who served as the 40th president from 1981 to 1989.

tossups.p: In 1947, this actor testified before the House Un-American Activities Committee while serving as president of the Screen Actors Guild. In the 1950s, he hosted _General Electric Theater_ on television and gave speeches at the company’s factories.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this former actor and governor of California who became president in 1981.

tossups.p: After this president was shot, Secretary of State Alexander Haig told reporters, “I am in control here.” Press secretary James Brady was also wounded in that attack, and a 1993 law requiring background checks for handgun buyers was later named for Brady.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this president who survived being shot by John Hinckley Jr. in 1981.

tossups.p: In August 1981, this president fired more than 11,000 air traffic controllers after their union, PATCO, went on strike in violation of a law banning strikes by federal workers. That same month, he signed a large cut in income tax rates.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Republican president who had been a Hollywood actor and governor of California.

tossups.p: In a 1983 speech to a meeting of evangelical Christians, this president called the Soviet Union an “evil empire.” About two weeks later, he proposed a missile defense system that critics nicknamed “Star Wars.”
tossups.r: That plan was the Strategic Defense Initiative. For 10 points, name this 40th president, who served from 1981 to 1989.

tossups.p: This president’s 1986 summit with Mikhail Gorbachev [“GOR-buh-chawf”] in Reykjavík [“RAYK-yuh-vik”], Iceland, nearly produced a deal to get rid of nuclear weapons, but it broke down over his missile defense plan. A year later, the two leaders signed the INF Treaty.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this president who, in Berlin, told Gorbachev to “tear down this wall.”

tossups.p: The Tower Commission investigated a scandal in which members of this president’s administration secretly sold weapons to Iran, hoping to free American hostages in Lebanon, and sent some of the profits to rebels fighting Nicaragua’s government, even though Congress had banned that aid. Marine officer Oliver North was a central figure in that affair.
tossups.r: Those rebels were called the Contras. For 10 points, name this president whose administration faced the Iran-Contra affair.

tossups.p: This president made William Rehnquist [“REN-kwist”] Chief Justice and appointed Antonin Scalia to the Supreme Court in 1986, but the Senate rejected his nominee Robert Bork the next year. Five years earlier, he had appointed the first woman to serve on the Supreme Court.
tossups.r: That woman was Sandra Day O’Connor. For 10 points, name this president who served from 1981 to 1989.

tossups.p: This president signed the Civil Liberties Act of 1988, which formally apologized to Japanese Americans who had been forced into camps during World War II. Two years earlier, he signed an immigration law that gave legal status to nearly three million people.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 40th president, a former actor and governor of California.

tossups.p: After the space shuttle _Challenger_ broke apart in 1986, this president said its crew had “slipped the surly bonds of earth” to “touch the face of God,” words from the poem “High Flight.” That night, he spoke from the Oval Office instead of giving his State of the Union address.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Republican president, a former actor and governor of California, who served from 1981 to 1989.

tossups.p: In a 1984 debate, this president promised not to exploit “my opponent’s youth and inexperience” for political purposes. That fall, he carried 49 states against Walter Mondale, after a campaign that included an ad declaring it was “morning again in America.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Republican, the oldest person elected president up to that time.

tossups.p: In his first inaugural address, this president said that “in this present crisis, government is not the solution to our problem; government is the problem.” Minutes after he took the oath of office, Iran released the 52 Americans it had held hostage for 444 days.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this president who had defeated Jimmy Carter in the 1980 election.

tossups.p: In a handwritten 1994 letter, this former president told Americans that he had Alzheimer’s disease. While in office, he had signed the 1983 law creating a national holiday honoring Martin Luther King Jr.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this president who told Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev to “tear down this wall” in 1987.

trap.title: Reagan or Bush?
trap.body: George H. W. Bush was Ronald Reagan’s vice president for all eight years and then became the 41st president, so 1980s Cold War clues can fit either man. The Berlin Wall actually fell in November 1989, during Bush’s first year, even though Reagan’s “Tear down this wall!” speech came in 1987. Iran clues are another trap: the hostage crisis belongs to Jimmy Carter, though the hostages were freed minutes after Reagan took office.
trap.fix: Reagan clues: acting, the Screen Actors Guild, governor of California, the 1981 assassination attempt, the air traffic controllers, “Reaganomics,” “evil empire,” SDI, Iran-Contra, and the INF Treaty. Bush clues: the fall of the Berlin Wall, the Persian Gulf War, and “Read my lips: no new taxes.” Terms named after him, like the Reagan Doctrine, are separate answers.
trap.line: Real answer line: Ronald Reagan (or Ronald Wilson Reagan)

topics.name: Rosa Parks
topics.kicker: Civil rights activist · Her 1955 arrest sparked the Montgomery Bus Boycott
topics.briefing: On December 1, 1955, Rosa Parks, a 42-year-old seamstress and secretary of the local NAACP, refused a bus driver’s order to give up her seat to a white passenger in Montgomery, Alabama, and was arrested. Her arrest sparked the Montgomery Bus Boycott, a 381-day protest led by a young Martin Luther King Jr. that ended after the courts struck down bus segregation. Congress later honored her as “the first lady of civil rights.”

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: A few months before her most famous act, this woman attended a workshop on ending segregation at the Highlander Folk School in Tennessee. She had served for years as secretary of her city’s NAACP chapter.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this woman whose arrest in Montgomery, Alabama, in December 1955 started a bus boycott.

tossups.p: In 1943, bus driver James F. Blake made this woman get off his bus so that she could re-enter through the back door, then drove away before she could get back on. She avoided riding his buses for years afterward.
tossups.r: In 1955, she refused Blake’s order to give up her seat. For 10 points, name this woman whose arrest led to the Montgomery Bus Boycott.

tossups.p: E. D. Nixon, a leader of the Brotherhood of Sleeping Car Porters, joined the white couple Clifford and Virginia Durr to bail this woman out of jail. Nixon believed her case was the right one to challenge her city’s segregated buses.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this seamstress whose arrest in Montgomery, Alabama, sparked a famous bus boycott.

tossups.p: Nine months before this woman’s arrest, a 15-year-old named Claudette Colvin was arrested for refusing to give up her seat on a bus in the same city. Colvin later became a plaintiff in _Browder v. Gayle_, the case that ended bus segregation there.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this woman who was arrested on a Montgomery bus on December 1, 1955.

tossups.p: Jo Ann Robinson and the Women’s Political Council stayed up all night printing leaflets after this woman’s arrest, calling on Black residents to stay off the buses on the day of her trial. That one-day protest grew into a boycott that lasted 381 days.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this woman whose refusal to give up her bus seat in Montgomery, Alabama, made her a symbol of the civil rights movement.

tossups.p: The lawyer Fred Gray defended this woman after her arrest, then filed _Browder v. Gayle_ on behalf of four other women who had faced discrimination on city buses. In that case, a federal court ruled that bus segregation in this woman’s city was unconstitutional.
tossups.r: The Supreme Court upheld that ruling in 1956. For 10 points, name this woman whose arrest started the Montgomery Bus Boycott.

tossups.p: In 2013, this woman became the first Black woman honored with a full-length statue in the U.S. Capitol. When she died in 2005, she became the first woman to lie in honor in the Capitol Rotunda.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this civil rights activist who refused to give up her bus seat in 1955.

tossups.p: This woman worked in the Detroit office of Congressman John Conyers for more than twenty years, beginning in 1965. The Henry Ford Museum in nearby Dearborn displays the city bus from her most famous moment.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this woman whose 1955 arrest in Montgomery, Alabama, led to a bus boycott.

tossups.p: This woman was riding the Cleveland Avenue bus home from her job as a seamstress at a department store when she made history. She later explained that she was not physically tired that evening: “the only tired I was, was tired of giving in.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this woman whose refusal to give up her seat sparked the Montgomery Bus Boycott.

tossups.p: This woman, born with the last name McCauley in Tuskegee [“tuh-SKEE-gee”], Alabama, grew up on her grandparents’ farm in Pine Level. She married a barber named Raymond who was active in the NAACP.
tossups.r: She later became secretary of the NAACP’s Montgomery branch. For 10 points, name this woman who was arrested on a Montgomery bus in 1955.

tossups.p: On December 5, 1955, this woman was found guilty of breaking her city’s bus segregation law and fined ten dollars plus court costs. That same day, a new group called the Montgomery Improvement Association chose a young minister as its leader.
tossups.r: That minister was Martin Luther King Jr. For 10 points, name this woman whose arrest started the Montgomery Bus Boycott.

tossups.p: This woman received the NAACP’s Spingarn Medal in 1979, the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 1996, and the Congressional Gold Medal in 1999. Congress also honored her as “the first lady of civil rights.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this woman whose arrest on a Montgomery bus in 1955 sparked a year-long boycott.

tossups.p: This woman wrote a 1992 autobiography with Jim Haskins and a 1994 book about her faith called _Quiet Strength_. She moved to Detroit in 1957 after losing her job and receiving threats in Alabama.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this woman whose refusal to give up her bus seat made her a symbol of the civil rights movement.

tossups.p: A well-known photograph of this woman being fingerprinted was actually taken in February 1956, when she and dozens of other boycott leaders were arrested under an old Alabama law against boycotts. Martin Luther King Jr. was also charged under that law.
tossups.r: Her first arrest had come months earlier on a city bus. For 10 points, name this woman whose arrest in December 1955 launched the Montgomery Bus Boycott.

tossups.p: In November 1956, the U.S. Supreme Court upheld a ruling against segregated buses in this woman’s city, and the boycott there ended about a month later. During that boycott, many Black residents walked or shared rides in carpools instead of riding the buses.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this woman whose refusal to give up her seat sparked the Montgomery Bus Boycott.

clues.t: Refused to give up her bus seat to a white passenger in Montgomery, Alabama, on December 1, 1955, and was arrested
Her arrest sparked the Montgomery Bus Boycott (1955–1956), led by Martin Luther King Jr.
Honored by Congress as “the first lady of civil rights” and “the mother of the freedom movement”
Secretary of the Montgomery branch of the NAACP
Said “the only tired I was, was tired of giving in”; she was not physically tired
The boycott lasted 381 days; many Black residents walked or carpooled instead of riding the buses
_Browder v. Gayle_ (1956) ruled Montgomery’s segregated buses unconstitutional, and the Supreme Court upheld it
Worked as a seamstress at the Montgomery Fair department store
Fifteen-year-old Claudette Colvin had refused to give up her seat nine months earlier
Moved to Detroit in 1957 and worked for Congressman John Conyers from 1965 to 1988
E. D. Nixon and Clifford and Virginia Durr bailed her out of jail
Jo Ann Robinson and the Women’s Political Council printed leaflets calling for the boycott
Driver James F. Blake ordered her to move; in 1943 he had driven off after making her get off to re-enter through the back door
Months before her arrest, attended a workshop on ending segregation at the Highlander Folk School in Tennessee
Was riding the Cleveland Avenue bus home from work
Lawyer Fred Gray defended her and filed _Browder v. Gayle_
_Browder v. Gayle_’s plaintiffs were Aurelia Browder, Susie McDonald, Claudette Colvin, and Mary Louise Smith, not her
Was convicted and fined $10 plus court costs on December 5, 1955, the first day of the boycott
Born Rosa Louise McCauley in Tuskegee, Alabama (1913); grew up on her grandparents’ farm in Pine Level
Her husband, Raymond, was a barber and an NAACP member
In 2005, became the first woman to lie in honor in the U.S. Capitol Rotunda
In 2013, became the first Black woman honored with a full-length statue in the U.S. Capitol
The bus from her arrest is displayed at the Henry Ford Museum in Dearborn, Michigan
Won the NAACP’s Spingarn Medal (1979), the Presidential Medal of Freedom (1996), and the Congressional Gold Medal (1999)
Wrote an autobiography with Jim Haskins (1992) and a book about her faith, _Quiet Strength_ (1994)
Her famous fingerprinting photo was taken in February 1956, when boycott leaders were arrested under an old anti-boycott law

trap.title: Woman, leader, or boycott?
trap.body: Several answer lines share this story. Claudette Colvin, a 15-year-old, refused to give up her seat on a Montgomery bus nine months before Rosa Parks did and later became a _Browder v. Gayle_ plaintiff. Martin Luther King Jr. led the boycott that Parks’s arrest started, and the Montgomery Bus Boycott itself is a separate answer, so listen for “this woman,” “this man,” or “this event.”
trap.fix: Parks clues: December 1, 1955, NAACP secretary, seamstress, the Highlander Folk School, James Blake, “tired of giving in,” and Detroit. Colvin clues: age 15, March 1955, and being a _Browder_ plaintiff. King clues: Dexter Avenue Baptist Church, the Montgomery Improvement Association, and “I Have a Dream.”
trap.line: Real answer line: Rosa Parks (or Rosa Louise McCauley Parks)
